title: Describe and apply the management functions of an organization

lessons.title: Planning and organising in practice
lessons.html:
Applying the management functions

Management is getting work done through people and other resources to achieve goals. The four classic functions are planning, organising, leading and controlling. This unit focuses on applying them in a supervisory role, such as running a slaughter shift, a deboning room or a grain intake point.

Planning

Planning is deciding in advance what to do, how, when and by whom. Good plans have SMART objectives: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

Example: 'Reduce carcass trim losses on the dressing line from 2.5% to 2% by the end of the quarter.'

Planning steps:

  1. Set the objective.
  2. Analyse the current situation and resources.
  3. Identify options and choose the best.
  4. Draw up an action plan: tasks, responsibilities, deadlines, resources.
  5. Communicate the plan.

Useful tools include a weekly production schedule, a staff roster, a maintenance calendar and a simple Gantt chart showing tasks across days.

Organising

Organising turns plans into a structure for work:

  • Break the work into tasks and stations.
  • Group tasks into jobs and assign people with the right skills.
  • Delegate authority and responsibility.
  • Provide tools, PPE, materials and information.
  • Coordinate with other sections such as maintenance, quality and dispatch.

A skills matrix, listing each worker against each task with their competence level, helps a supervisor assign people and plan multi-skilling so that the line can run when someone is absent.

Delegation

Delegating means giving someone a task with the authority to complete it, while you remain accountable. Delegate clearly: explain the task, standard, deadline and limits of authority, then check progress without micromanaging.

lessons.title: Leading and motivating people
lessons.html:
Leading a team

Leading is influencing people to work willingly towards goals. In a high-pressure environment like a slaughter line, the supervisor's leadership has a direct effect on safety, quality and output.

Leadership styles

StyleDescriptionWhen it fits
Directive (autocratic)Leader decides and instructsEmergencies, safety-critical situations, new untrained workers
Participative (democratic)Leader involves team in decisionsImproving processes, planning rosters, solving recurring problems
Delegating (free-rein)Team decides within boundariesExperienced, competent, motivated teams

Situational leadership means adapting your style to the person and situation rather than using one style for everything.

Motivation

People are motivated by different things. Maslow's hierarchy suggests basic needs (pay, safety) must be met before higher needs (belonging, recognition, growth) motivate. Herzberg separated hygiene factors, such as pay, conditions and fair supervision, which cause dissatisfaction when poor, from motivators, such as achievement, recognition and responsibility, which drive real motivation.

Practical motivators for a supervisor:

  • Recognise good work publicly and specifically.
  • Give workers responsibility and chances to learn new stations.
  • Explain why targets and rules matter.
  • Treat everyone fairly and consistently.
  • Fix hygiene factors you can influence, such as broken equipment or poor PPE.

Communication

Leaders communicate constantly: shift briefings, toolbox talks, one-on-one conversations and notice boards. Keep messages clear, check understanding and listen to feedback. In multilingual teams, use simple language and ask team members to help explain where needed.

Teamwork

Build team spirit by setting shared goals, celebrating team achievements such as injury-free months, and dealing quickly with conflict.

lessons.title: Controlling performance
lessons.html:
The control process

Controlling ensures that actual performance matches the plan. It has four steps:

  1. Set standards: for example, throughput per hour, yield percentage, maximum defects, zero lost-time injuries, cleaning standards.
  2. Measure performance: through counts, scales, inspection results, records and observation.
  3. Compare actual results with standards and identify deviations.
  4. Take corrective action: find the cause and fix it, or revise the standard if it was unrealistic.

Types of control

  • Feedforward (preventive): before work starts, such as pre-start equipment checks and checking incoming livestock documents.
  • Concurrent: during work, such as monitoring line speed and carcass hygiene on the line.
  • Feedback: after work, such as daily yield reports and customer complaints.

Key performance areas for a supervisor

AreaExample measure
OutputCarcasses per hour, tons received
QualityContamination findings, rework, customer complaints
CostOvertime hours, water and electricity use, packaging waste
SafetyIncidents, near misses, PPE compliance
PeopleAbsenteeism, training completed, staff turnover

Budgets as a control tool

Supervisors often manage part of a budget, such as overtime or consumables. Compare actual spending with the budget each month and explain variances. For example, if overtime is above budget because of a breakdown, report the cause and the plan to recover.

Problem solving

When a deviation appears, use a simple method: define the problem, gather facts, find the root cause by asking 'why' several times, choose a solution, implement it and check the result. Involve the team, because they often know the cause.

Key points

  • Plans should have SMART objectives and clear action plans.
  • Organising means assigning tasks, delegating authority and providing resources.
  • Adapt your leadership style to the person and situation.
  • Recognition, responsibility and fairness are strong motivators.
  • Control by setting standards, measuring, comparing and correcting.
